name: Core
title: Core
summary: The Core validates your BeNomad license, then deploys and loads the map data and the other resources the SDK needs.
text:
# Core

The Core validates your BeNomad license, then deploys and loads the map data and the other resources the SDK needs. Almost every other module requires it. It takes a purchase UUID, provided by BeNomad, which sets the maps to download (HERE, TomTom, OpenStreetMap, etc.), the number of installations allowed, the deployment mode (full or hybrid maps) and the map coverage.

These modules depend on the Core: AndroidAuto, Geocoder, GpsManager, MapServices, Mapping, Navigation, Planner, TrafficManager and VehicleManager, and the internal modules BeMapAPI and SettingsManager.

**Internet connection:** the first initialization of the Core needs one. After that, the Core must be initialized online again before the end of each authorized offline period (30 days by default): see *`OnOfflinePeriodExpiredCallback`* below.

## Dependencies

This module depends on these BeNomad modules:

- Error Manager

Its third-party libraries are declared in its published POM, so Gradle adds them to your app. The module is built with these versions:

| Library | Version |
|---|---|
| `androidx.appcompat:appcompat` | 1.8.0 |
| `com.google.android.material:material` | 1.14.0 |
| `androidx.core:core-ktx` | 1.18.0 |
| `org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-stdlib` | 2.4.20 |
| `org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-android` | 1.11.0 |
| `org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-core` | 1.11.0 |

Declare one yourself only if your code uses its types directly.

Your app needs `minSdk` 24 or higher and core library desugaring: see *Configure your app module* on the main page of the SDK documentation.

**Release builds minified with R8:** the SDK's native code finds the SDK's classes, constructors, methods and fields by their names. If your app enables R8 (`minifyEnabled true`), keep them, for example with this rule in your app's ProGuard rules file:

```
-keep class com.benomad.msdk.** { *; }
```

## Permissions

- **`READ_PHONE_STATE`**, below Android 10: request it before initializing the Core. The license validation needs it.
- **`WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE`**, optional, below Android 11: only to deploy the maps outside your app's scoped storage.
- **`INTERNET`**: declare it in your manifest.

The Permissions Manager module can request these permissions for you. Using it is optional.

### Device identifier

The license is tied to a device identifier, which the Core reads at each initialization. By default:

- from Android 10, it is the `ANDROID_ID`;
- below Android 10, it is the IMEI (hence the `READ_PHONE_STATE` permission), or else the Wi-Fi MAC address, or else the `ANDROID_ID`.

To read the MAC address while Wi-Fi is off, the Core switches Wi-Fi on for a few seconds, then off again. To prevent this, add this entry to the `<application>` element of your manifest; the Core then never uses the MAC address:

```xml
<meta-data android:name="wifi_access" android:value="false" />
```

## Core initialization

This sample initializes the Core:

```kotlin
import com.benomad.msdk.core.Core
import com.benomad.msdk.core.callbacks.OnCoreInit.OnCoreInitCallback
import com.benomad.msdk.errormanager.Error

// Receives the result of the Core initialization, on the main thread
val coreInitCallback = object : OnCoreInitCallback {
    override fun onCoreReady() {
        // The Core is initialized: the other modules can be used
    }
    override fun onCoreInitError(error: Error) {
        // The initialization failed: see CoreErrorCodes
    }
    override fun onCoreInitException(exception: Exception) {
        // An exception was raised during the initialization
    }
}

// Below Android 10, the READ_PHONE_STATE permission must have been granted first.
// init returns at once; the result reaches coreInitCallback later.
val core = Core.getInstance()
if (!core.isInit()) {
    core.init(
        applicationContext = applicationContext,
        purchaseUUID = purchaseUUID,
        licenseKey = null,
        mapsDeploymentPath = core.getDefaultMapsPath(applicationContext),
        resourcesPathInAssets = core.getDefaultAssetsResourcesPath(),
        mapsPathInAssets = null,
        callback = coreInitCallback
    )
}
```

The arguments of `init`:

- `applicationContext`: the application context.
- `purchaseUUID`: your BeNomad purchase UUID. Required: without it, the initialization fails.
- `licenseKey`: optional. Forces the activation with this license key; pass null to activate with the purchase UUID only.
- `mapsDeploymentPath`: the absolute path where the maps are deployed. Maps already deployed there are used as they are, and not downloaded. Without a value, the maps go to a "Maps" folder in your app's external scoped storage (its "files" folder).
- `resourcesPathInAssets`: the path of the resources folder, relative to the assets folder. The Mapping module needs these resources; pass null if you don't deploy them.
- `mapsPathInAssets`: the path of a maps folder to deploy, relative to the assets folder. With null, the Core downloads the maps from BeNomad's servers when it finds none in `mapsDeploymentPath`.
- `callback`: the `OnCoreInitCallback` that receives the result of the initialization.

### Where to deploy the maps

Store the maps in the default `mapsDeploymentPath`: your app's external scoped storage, in the internal memory of the device. `Core.getInstance().getDefaultMapsPath(context)` returns it.

- A path outside your app's scoped storage works only below Android 11, and requires the `WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` permission before the Core is initialized.
- On an SD card, deploy the map data yourself before initializing the Core: automatic online deployment to an SD card isn't supported. See *Manual update or initial deployment* below.

## Map data deployment
### Automatic online deployment

When no map data is deployed before the initialization, nor during it with the `mapsPathInAssets` argument of `Core.init`, the Core deploys the map data automatically if the device is online. This doesn't work on an SD card.

Online map updates go through four callbacks, described under *Observables (callbacks)* below:

1. `OnMapUpdateAvailableCallback` tells you that an update is available. Accept or decline it.
2. `OnMapDownloadProgressCallback` reports the progress of the download.
3. `OnMapDownloadErrorCallback` reports an error during the download.
4. `OnMapDownloadedCallback` tells you that the download has finished.

The downloaded update is then staged. It is applied when the app starts again and initializes the Core, usually at the next launch: `Core.init` can't be called again in a running process. *The OTA map update process in detail* below gives the full sequence, including the map extraction progress.

### Manual update or initial deployment

To deploy or update map data yourself (from an SD card, for example), put it in `mapsDeploymentPath`, or replace the data there, before initializing the Core. The deployed map package must contain the **mapsversion** file: without it, the licensing system replaces the map data you deployed.

On an SD card, with an app targeting Android 11 or higher, deploy the map data into your app's external scoped storage on the SD card. For example, if your app's external scoped storage is:

- `/sdcard/Android/data/com.example.app/files` (also reachable as `/storage/self/primary/Android/data/com.example.app/files`), in the internal memory,

then its counterpart on the SD card, where to deploy the map data, is:

- `/storage/sdcard1/Android/data/com.example.app/files/`.

Android Studio's Device File Explorer shows these paths: `/sdcard/Android/data/` (or `/storage/self/primary/Android/`) is the internal memory, where apps keep their data, and `/storage/sdcard1/Android/data/` is the SD card, where they can keep data too.

## The OTA map update process in detail

*Observables (callbacks)* below documents each callback on its own. This section shows how they fit together: in what order they fire, and what your app has to do, so that you can implement map updates end to end.

### How map data reaches the device

Map data comes from BeNomad's servers. When no maps are deployed yet, the Core downloads them; it also keeps deployed maps up to date by downloading newer versions when they are published.

The deployment mode (full or hybrid maps) is set by your purchase UUID, not chosen at runtime. `Core.getInstance().isUsingHybridMaps()` doesn't report it: after the initialization, it returns true only while the loaded maps still contain partial files.

Two rules apply to every callback below:

- **They are all delivered on the main (UI) thread.** You can update your UI from them, but don't run long or blocking work in them: it would freeze the UI.
- **Register your observers before calling `Core.init(...)`.** Some events fire early in the initialization, and an observer added later misses them. The Core keeps strong references to its observers and never removes them: call the matching `removeOn...Observer(...)` when the observer's owner (an Activity or a Fragment, for example) is destroyed, or you leak it.

### How updates are applied

An online update never replaces the maps of a running app. The new data is downloaded and prepared in a separate staging area, while the maps in use stay untouched. The staged update becomes active only when the app starts again and calls `Core.init(...)`, usually at the next launch.

So:

- your app keeps using the current maps until it restarts;
- an interrupted or failed update can't corrupt the maps in use: they are swapped only after a fully successful download;
- the user gets the update at the next launch of the app.

The one exception is the very first deployment, when the device has no maps yet: it is applied at once, during the same `init`, because there are no maps in use to protect.

### Online update lifecycle, step by step

This is the flow when maps are already deployed and a newer version exists on BeNomad's servers. Each arrow is a callback you can observe:

```
Core.init(...)  --->  onCoreReady()                    app runs on the current maps
      |
      |  (the Core checks for a newer version in the background)
      v
onMapUpdateAvailable()                                 a newer map version exists on the server
      |
      |  YOUR decision, in response to the callback:
      |     downloadAvailableUpdate(true)    accept and start the download
      |     downloadAvailableUpdate(false)   decline
      v
onMapDownloadProgress(progress, downloaded, total)    repeated while the package downloads (sizes in KB)
      v
onMapExtractionProgress(progress)                     repeated while the downloaded package is unpacked
      v
onMapDownloaded()                                     update fully downloaded and staged (NOT active yet)
      |
      |  ... the app keeps running on the OLD maps ...
      v
(next launch) Core.init(...)  --->  onCoreReady()     staged update is applied; app now runs on the NEW maps
```

1. **Availability.** After the initialization, the Core checks for a newer map version in the background, periodically rather than continuously: by default, about once every 24 hours after the app started. So `onMapUpdateAvailable()` can arrive at any time while your app runs, not only right after `init`: another reason to register the observer up front.
2. **Your decision.** The download doesn't start on its own. In `onMapUpdateAvailable()`, call `Core.getInstance().downloadAvailableUpdate(true)` to start it, or `downloadAvailableUpdate(false)` to decline. Call this method only after `onMapUpdateAvailable()` has fired.
3. **Download.** While the package downloads, you receive `onMapDownloadProgress(progress, downloaded, total)`: `progress` runs from 0 to 100, and `downloaded` and `total` are sizes in kilobytes.
4. **Preparation.** The downloaded package is unpacked and prepared; `onMapExtractionProgress(progress)` reports this step, from 0 to 100.
5. **Staged.** `onMapDownloaded()` fires once the update is fully downloaded and staged. Your running app still uses the previous maps.
6. **Activation.** At the next launch, `Core.init(...)` swaps the staged update into place, and `onCoreReady()` is called with the new maps active.

The initial online download, described next, reports its progress through the same `onMapDownloadProgress`: one progress handler serves both cases.

### Initial online deployment vs updates

When no maps are deployed, none are bundled in `assets`, and the device is online, the Core downloads the maps during `init` itself. This first deployment differs from an update:

- you don't receive `onMapUpdateAvailable()`, and you don't call `downloadAvailableUpdate(...)`;
- `onMapDownloadProgress(...)` and `onMapExtractionProgress(...)` fire during `init`, before `onCoreReady()`;
- the maps are deployed at once, and are active as soon as `init` finishes.

So `onMapDownloaded()` means "the initial maps are downloaded and active" in the first case, and "the update is downloaded and staged for the next launch" in the second. No flag tells them apart: check whether you had already reached `onCoreReady()` with working maps.
Automatic online deployment doesn't work on an SD card (see *Manual update or initial deployment* above).

### Simulating a map update for testing

To test your map download handling without waiting for BeNomad to publish a newer map version, make the Core download the maps again: delete the `mapsversion` file at the root of the deployed maps folder. That folder is the `mapsDeploymentPath` you passed to `Core.init`; by default, the `Maps` folder that `Core.getInstance().getDefaultMapsPath(context)` returns.

Without that file, the licensing system can no longer identify the version of the maps on the device. At the next `Core.init`, it treats them as maps to redeploy and downloads them again from BeNomad's servers: the behavior *Manual update or initial deployment* above warns about, used here on purpose. The device must be online.

You then receive the same callbacks as for a server download: `onMapDownloadProgress(...)`, then `onMapExtractionProgress(...)`, then `onMapDownloaded()`, and can test your progress UI and your completion handling end to end.
Do this during development only: never delete the `mapsversion` file in a shipping app, because it forces a full download of the map data.

### Error handling during the map update

Two callbacks report problems, depending on the error:

- `onMapDownloadError(error)`: download and preparation failures, such as a network failure during the download, not enough storage space, or an unpacking failure;
- `onLicenseError(error)`: licensing failures.

The Core retries a failing download several times before it reports an error. As the maps are swapped only after a fully successful download, a failed or aborted update leaves the deployed maps intact and usable.
When the licensing server can't be reached but a valid cached license exists, the Core uses the cached license and reports no error (see *`OnOfflinePeriodExpiredCallback`* below).

### Hybrid maps (on-demand map data)

With hybrid maps, the map data ships partial, and the rest is downloaded on demand as the map is used. After `onCoreReady()`, `Core.getInstance().isUsingHybridMaps()` returns true while the loaded maps still contain partial files.
These on-demand downloads are separate from the map update flow above:

- Their progress comes through `onHybridMapDownloadProgress(status, progress)`, not `onMapDownloadProgress`, with its own status codes: -3 not enough storage, -2 internal error, -1 download failed, 0 started, 1 in progress, 2 finished. `progress` is negative on errors.
- `loadFullMapsInArea(area, asyncMode)` downloads the full map data of a rectangular area, and `loadFullMapsInCountry(countryCode, asyncMode)` that of a country (ISO 3166 Alpha-3 code). Both return an `Error?`:
  - `CORE_NOT_YET_INITIALIZED` if the Core isn't ready;
  - `CORE_NOT_USING_HYBRID_MAPS` if `isUsingHybridMaps()` returns false;
  - null otherwise. Null means that the download was requested, not that it succeeded.

  `asyncMode` defaults to false: the call then blocks until the download finishes, so don't make it on the main thread.
- `cancelPendingHybridDownloads()` cancels the queued hybrid downloads.

### Implementation checklist and full sample

1. Register the observers you need before calling `Core.init(...)`: at least `addOnMapUpdateAvailableObserver`, `addOnMapDownloadProgressObserver`, `addOnMapExtractionProgressObserver`, `addOnMapDownloadedObserver` and `addOnMapDownloadErrorObserver`.
2. Call `Core.init(...)` once per process. A call made while an initialization is running is refused with a BUSY error.
3. In `onMapUpdateAvailable()`, ask the user, then call `downloadAvailableUpdate(true)` or `downloadAvailableUpdate(false)`.
4. Drive your progress UI from `onMapDownloadProgress`, then from `onMapExtractionProgress`.
5. In `onMapDownloaded()`, tell the user that the update applies at the next launch: the new maps aren't live yet.
6. The staged update becomes active when the app restarts, usually at the next launch. Don't call `Core.init(...)` again in the running process.
7. Handle `onMapDownloadError` and `onLicenseError`.
8. Remove your observers when their owner is destroyed.

```kotlin
import com.benomad.msdk.core.Core
import com.benomad.msdk.core.callbacks.OnMapUpdateAvailable.OnMapUpdateAvailableCallback
import com.benomad.msdk.core.callbacks.OnMapDownloadProgress.OnMapDownloadProgressCallback
import com.benomad.msdk.core.callbacks.OnMapExtractionProgress.OnMapExtractionProgressCallback
import com.benomad.msdk.core.callbacks.OnMapDownloaded.OnMapDownloadedCallback
import com.benomad.msdk.core.callbacks.OnMapDownloadError.OnMapDownloadErrorCallback
import com.benomad.msdk.errormanager.Error

class MapUpdateHandler(
    private val core: Core = Core.getInstance()
) : OnMapUpdateAvailableCallback,
    OnMapDownloadProgressCallback,
    OnMapExtractionProgressCallback,
    OnMapDownloadedCallback,
    OnMapDownloadErrorCallback {

    // Call this BEFORE core.init(...)
    fun register() {
        core.addOnMapUpdateAvailableObserver(this)
        core.addOnMapDownloadProgressObserver(this)
        core.addOnMapExtractionProgressObserver(this)
        core.addOnMapDownloadedObserver(this)
        core.addOnMapDownloadErrorObserver(this)
    }

    // Call this when your owner (Activity or Fragment) is destroyed
    fun unregister() {
        core.removeOnMapUpdateAvailableObserver(this)
        core.removeOnMapDownloadProgressObserver(this)
        core.removeOnMapExtractionProgressObserver(this)
        core.removeOnMapDownloadedObserver(this)
        core.removeOnMapDownloadErrorObserver(this)
    }

    // A newer map version is available on the server. Ask the user, then decide.
    override fun onMapUpdateAvailable() {
        val userAccepted = askUserToUpdate() // your own UI
        core.downloadAvailableUpdate(userAccepted)
    }

    // All callbacks below are delivered on the main thread.
    override fun onMapDownloadProgress(progress: Float, downloaded: Float, total: Float) {
        // progress: 0..100, downloaded and total in KB
    }

    override fun onMapExtractionProgress(progress: Float) {
        // progress: 0..100 (unpacking the downloaded package)
    }

    override fun onMapDownloaded() {
        // The update is downloaded and staged. It becomes active at the next app launch.
        // Tell the user to restart the app.
    }

    override fun onMapDownloadError(error: Error) {
        // Download or preparation failed. The maps currently in use are left intact.
    }

    private fun askUserToUpdate(): Boolean = true
}
```

## Observables (callbacks)

Each observer is added with `Core.getInstance().addOn…Observer(...)`. Register them before initializing the Core. In the samples below, `this` implements the callback interface; an object works too.

### `OnInitProgressCallback`: map loading progress

The loading of the maps is the last step of the Core initialization.

```kotlin
Core.getInstance().addOnInitProgressObserver(this) 
    // the observer parameter in this example is the class that implements the OnInitProgressCallback, but it can also be an object variable

override fun onInitProgress(progress: Float) {
    // progress of the loading of the maps, the last step of the Core initialization, from 0 to 100
}

```

### `OnMapDownloadProgressCallback`: map download progress

It reports the initial download and the downloads of updates.

```kotlin
Core.getInstance().addOnMapDownloadProgressObserver(this)

override fun onMapDownloadProgress(progress: Float, downloaded: Float, total: Float) {
    //progress is the current progress of the maps download from 0 to 100
    //downloaded is the size in KB of the data already downloaded
    //total is the total size in KB to download
}

```

### `OnHybridMapDownloadProgressCallback`: hybrid map download progress

Only with hybrid maps.

```kotlin
Core.getInstance().addOnHybridDownloadProgressObserver(this)

override fun onHybridMapDownloadProgress(status: Int, progress: Double) {
    //status is the current status of the hybrid download
    /**
        -3: Not enough storage space,
        -2: Internal error,
        -1: Download failed (network error), 
         0: Download started, 
         1: Download in progress and the percentage is available, 
         2: Download finished
     */
    
    //progress is the current progress of the maps download from 0 to 100; it is negative on errors
}
```

### `OnMapExtractionProgressCallback`: map extraction progress

It reports the unpacking of a downloaded map package.

```kotlin
Core.getInstance().addOnMapExtractionProgressObserver(this)

override fun onMapExtractionProgress(progress: Float) {
   //progress is the current progress of the map extraction from 0 to 100
}

```

### `OnLicenseErrorCallback`: license errors

```kotlin
import com.benomad.msdk.errormanager.Error

Core.getInstance().addOnLicenseErrorObserver(this)

override fun onLicenseError(error: Error) {
    val messageId = error.messageId // the message id of the error
    val errorExplanation = error.detailedMessage // a more detailed message about the error (not always available, in this case an empty String is returned)
}

```

### `OnMapUpdateAvailableCallback`: a map update is available

The progress of the update's download then comes through `OnMapDownloadProgressCallback`, as for the initial download.

```kotlin
Core.getInstance().addOnMapUpdateAvailableObserver(this)

override fun onMapUpdateAvailable() {
    //a map update is available.
    Core.getInstance().downloadAvailableUpdate(userChoice) //user choice is a Boolean that indicates if the user accepted the update download or refused it.
}

```

### `OnMapDownloadedCallback`: maps downloaded

Called when the initial maps or an update are downloaded. An update is installed at the next start of the app.

```kotlin
Core.getInstance().addOnMapDownloadedObserver(this)

override fun onMapDownloaded() {
    //the initial map download or the map update download has finished. In case of an update, it will be installed on next application start
}

```

### `OnMapDownloadErrorCallback`: map download errors

For the initial download and for updates.

```kotlin
import com.benomad.msdk.errormanager.Error

Core.getInstance().addOnMapDownloadErrorObserver(this)

override fun onMapDownloadError(error: Error) {
    //called if something happened during the map download (connection error, no space available, unzipping, etc)
    val messageId = error.messageId // the message id of the error
    val errorExplanation = error.detailedMessage // a more detailed message about the error (not always available, in this case an empty String is returned)
}

```

### `OnOfflinePeriodExpiredCallback`: offline period expired

The first initialization of the Core needs an Internet connection. After it, the Core can be initialized offline during an authorized offline period. When that period has expired, `onOfflinePeriodExpired` is called: the Core can no longer be initialized offline, because it must validate your license with BeNomad's licensing system. The next online initialization starts a new offline period.

```kotlin
Core.getInstance().addOnOfflinePeriodExpiredObserver(this)

override fun onOfflinePeriodExpired() {
    //this is triggered when the offline period has expired
    //you have to initialize the Core with an active internet connection, otherwise the Core won't be initialized anymore
}
```

name: Mapping

summary: The Mapping module provides interactive maps as Android views.
text:
# Mapping

The Mapping module provides interactive maps as Android views. The maps show the map data deployed by the Core, from the cartographic provider set by the UUID (license provided by BeNomad) that initializes the Core. An app can show several maps, each with its own style. Users interact with a map through gestures (tap, double tap, long press, pan, pinch, rotate, tilt), and dynamic layers add points, lines, polylines, rectangles, ellipses, polygons, corridors and more.

*The maps need resources that you deploy from the assets when you initialize the Core (its `resourcesPathInAssets` argument): see the **Core initialization** section of the Core module.*

## Dependencies

This module depends on these BeNomad modules:

- Error Manager
- Core
- Settings Manager (internal module)
- Geocoder (the `Address` class of the map click results)
- Vehicle Manager (the `Profile` class of `showRoadRestrictions`)

Its third-party libraries are declared in its published POM, so Gradle adds them to your app. The module is built with these versions:

| Library | Version |
|---|---|
| `androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-ktx` | 2.11.0 |
| `org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-stdlib` | 2.4.20 |
| `androidx.core:core-ktx` | 1.18.0 |
| `androidx.appcompat:appcompat` | 1.8.0 |
| `com.google.android.material:material` | 1.14.0 |

Declare one yourself only if your code uses its types directly.

**Release builds minified with R8:** the SDK's native code finds the SDK's classes, constructors, methods and fields by their names, for example the classes of this module's map click results. If your app enables R8 (`minifyEnabled true`), keep them, for example with this rule in your app's ProGuard rules file:

```
-keep class com.benomad.msdk.** { *; }
```

## Using a MapView

Add a `MapView` member to your Activity or Fragment. Alternatively, use `MapViewFragment`, which wraps a `MapView` and restores its `MapState` across configuration changes.

``` kotlin
private lateinit var mapView: MapView
```

Create the `MapView` once your Activity or Fragment view exists, and add it to your layout. Its map is created only once the view is attached to a window, visible and laid out.

``` kotlin
mapView = MapView(requireContext(), callback = this) //the callback argument is the Activity/Fragment that implements the OnMapReadyCallback
mapContainer.addView(mapView) //mapContainer is a ViewGroup of your layout, for example a FrameLayout
```

### The MapView constructor

- `context`: the context of the Activity or Fragment that uses the view.
- `attrs`: the XML attributes of the view when it is inflated from a layout, `null` otherwise. As it is the second parameter, pass the optional arguments after it by name.
- `gestureOptions`: optional, a `GestureOptions` that sets which gestures are enabled. Without it, all gestures are enabled.
- `onGestureListener`: optional, an `OnGestureListener` notified of the gesture events of the `MapView` (for example, a double tap).
- `onStateChanged`: optional suspending function called with the new `MapState` when the camera of the map changes, on a background thread, at most about once every 200 ms. It can skip states, including the last one of a gesture: to know where the camera stopped, call `getCurrentMapState()` on the main thread.
- `callback`: an `OnMapReadyCallback`, notified when the map is ready to be used, or when its initialization failed.

*A `MapView` declared in the XML layout needs no constructor call: see the "Mapping and POI" sample.*

This example passes 4 arguments, the optional ones by name:

``` kotlin
import com.benomad.msdk.errormanager.Error // the Error class of the MSDK, not kotlin.Error

val onMapReadyCallback = object : OnMapReadyCallback{
    override fun onMapReady() {
		// map is ready to be manipulated
    }

    override fun onMapError(error: Error) {
        // an error occurred during the map initialization
        val messageId = error.messageId // the message id of the error
        val errorExplanation = error.detailedMessage // a more detailed message about the error (not always available, in this case an empty String is returned)
    }
}

val gestureOptions = GestureOptions() // by default all gestures are enabled
gestureOptions.setGestureStatus(Gesture.DOUBLE_TAP, false) // disable the double tap gesture

val gestureListener = object : OnGestureListener {
    override fun onTapEvent(point: PointF) {
    }

    override fun onDoubleTapEvent(point: PointF) {
    }

    override fun onLongPressEvent(point: PointF) {
    }

    override fun onPanStart() {
    }

    override fun onPanEnd() {
    }

    override fun onPinchZoomEvent(scaleFactor: Double) {
    }

    override fun onRotateEvent(angle: Double) {
    }

    override fun onTiltEvent(angle: Double) {
    }
}

mapView = MapView(requireContext(), gestureOptions = gestureOptions, onGestureListener = gestureListener, callback = onMapReadyCallback)
mapContainer.addView(mapView) // add the MapView to your layout (mapContainer is a ViewGroup of your layout)
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(mapView) // make the MapView observe the activity lifecycle to automatically call the onDestroy method of the MapView when the OnDestroy cycle of the activity is triggered (the OnDestroyView cycle in case of a Fragment)

```

Several observers can receive the result of the `MapView` initialization. Add them right after building the `MapView`: an observer added once the map is ready isn't called.

```kotlin
mapView.addOnMapReadyObserver(observer) // an observer of type OnMapReadyCallback
```

Remove them on the matching lifecycle event:

``` 
mapView.removeOnMapReadyObserver(observer)
```

### Lifecycle of a MapView

- Create the `MapView` on the main thread. Its map is created once the Core is initialized and the view is attached to a window, visible and laid out: `onMapReady()` is then called on the main thread.
- Destroy the `MapView` when you no longer need it: call `mapView.onDestroy()` on the main thread, or let the `MapView` observe the lifecycle as in the example above. Until then, the view, its context and its map stay in memory. A destroyed `MapView` can't be used again: create a new one.
- Don't call the `onPause()` and `onResume()` methods that `MapView` inherits from `GLSurfaceView`: the view manages its rendering itself.
- Don't move the `MapView` to another parent, and don't remove it from its window to add it back later: to show the map somewhere else, destroy the `MapView` and create a new one.
- If the map is attached to the Navigation module (`attachMapView`), stop the guidance session (`stopSession`) before destroying the `MapView`.

## Map states

A `MapState` holds the camera of a map: its center, tilt, zoom level and orientation. Build one to apply it to the `MapView`, or read the current one:

``` kotlin
val mapCenter = GeoPoint(3.24, 43.6) //defines a GeoPoint to center the map on
val tiltAngle = 60.0 // defines the tilt angle of the map in degrees
val zoomLevel = 15.2 //defines the zoom level of the map, between mapView.minZoomLevel and mapView.maxZoomLevel (see the note on zoom levels below)
val orientation = 20.0 // defines the map orientation in degrees

val mapState = MapState(mapCenter, tiltAngle, zoomLevel, orientation) 
mapView.updateMapState(mapState) //updates the MapView with the created MapState

MapView.Companion.setDefaultMapState(applicationContext, mapState) //save a default MapState using the SharedPreferences
val defaultMapState = MapView.Companion.getDefaultMapState(applicationContext) //get the saved default MapState

```

Call `updateMapState` and `getCurrentMapState` only once the map is ready. To set the camera when the map becomes ready, do it in an observer added with `addOnMapReadyObserver` right after building the `MapView`: that observer is notified after the view has re-applied its own saved state.

The current `MapState` of the `MapView`:

``` kotlin
val currentMapState = mapView.getCurrentMapState()
```

### Note on zoom levels

- At zoom level 0, the whole Earth is visible, from the South to the North pole, whatever the screen's size and density.
- Each zoom level doubles the scale of the previous one: at zoom level *n*, a pixel covers half as many meters as at zoom level *n-1*.

To zoom without a `MapState`:

``` kotlin
mapView.zoom(zoomLevel, true) //zoom to the given zoomLevel and redraw the map
```

The current zoom level of the `MapView`:

``` kotlin
val currentZoomLevel = mapView.zoomLevel
```

The API reference lists the other methods.

## Map parameters

### Double tap behavior

By default, a double tap zooms in towards the tapped point. To zoom on the center of the map instead:

```kotlin
mapView.useMapCenterForDoubleTap = true
```

### Double tap zoom scale

The zoom scale of a double tap:

``` kotlin
mapView.doubleTapZoomScale = 2.0
```

### Double tap animation speed

The speed of the zoom animation of a double tap:

``` kotlin
mapView.doubleTapZoomScaleStep = 0.2 //zoom animation is now 2x quicker (initial value is 0.1)
```

*The default value is 0.1, and the value must be greater than 0: a lower value slows the animation down, a higher value speeds it up.*

### Maximum tilt angle

The maximum tilt angle of the `MapView`:

``` kotlin
mapView.maxTiltAngle = 50.0 //set the maximum tilt angle to 50 degrees
```

## Map style

The styles of the map (graphic charts) are defined by .cht files provided by BeNomad. They must be deployed in the app's storage to be used: we recommend putting all .cht files in the resources folder that the Core deploys (see the Core module for the deployment of the resources).

To change the style of the `MapView`, apply a .cht file:

````kotlin
val chartFile = File(getExternalFilesDir(null), "day.cht") //the path to the day.cht file already deployed in the external scoped storage of the application (files directory)
val baseDir = File(getExternalFilesDir(null), "") //the path to the base directory

val styleLoader = MapStyleLoader //used for loading the styles
val loadingError = styleLoader.loadStyle("DAY_STYLE", chartFile, baseDir) // loads the style from the day.cht file: returns null on success, or an Error
styleLoader.getStyle("DAY_STYLE")?.let { style -> mapView.setMapStyle(style) } // Apply the loaded 'DAY_STYLE' to the MapView (getStyle returns null if no style is loaded with this name)

````

## Layers style

*Load at least one map style, as described above, before creating layer styles.*

On top of the styles of the .cht file, you can add styles for some types of layers:

- POI style, with `createPOIStyle`:

  ``` kotlin
  //using the sample example as above
  val loadedStyle = MapStyleLoader.getStyle("DAY_STYLE")
  val iconPath = File(baseDir, "my_poi_icon.png").absolutePath // a PNG file deployed with the map resources
  val styleCreationResult = loadedStyle?.createPOIStyle(12001, POIStyle(icon = iconPath)) // null on success, or an Error. The new POI style of the classID 12001 draws this icon; its other options keep the default values of the POIStyle constructor. See the API reference for more details about the POIStyle class.
  ```

- Polyline style, with `createPolylineStyle`:

  ``` kotlin
  val styleCreationResult = loadedStyle?.createPolylineStyle(12002, PolylineStyle())
  ```

- Polygon style, with `createPolygonStyle`:

  ``` kotlin
  val styleCreationResult = loadedStyle?.createPolygonStyle(12003, ClosedStyle())
  ```

*A created style can't be changed, but it can be deleted with its class ID, for example `loadedStyle?.deleteStyle(12001)`. `deleteStyle` returns no result: it doesn't tell whether a style was deleted.*

## Add POIs and other layers to the map

You can add POIs, and other layers, to a `MapView`. Every layer you add to the map has a class ID:

- The maps already define cartographic class IDs, and you can use them for your layers: these layers are then drawn with the style of that class ID. The `CartoConst` class of the Core module lists most of them.
- You can also use your own class ID, as long as it isn't one of the maps' class IDs. By convention, custom class IDs are between 12000 and 12999, a range no class of the maps uses.
- The class ID sets the z-index: a layer with a higher class ID is drawn on top. For example, a layer of class ID 10003L is drawn on top of all layers whose class ID is lower than 10003L.

To add them, create a group of layers once the Core is initialized, and attach it once the map is ready (in `onMapReady`). A layer is drawn only if its class ID has a style (see *Layers style*): here, the POI style created above for the class ID 12001.

``` kotlin
import com.benomad.msdk.core.carto.CartoConst
import com.benomad.msdk.core.svs.Attribute
import com.benomad.msdk.core.svs.DynamicLayersGroup
import com.benomad.msdk.core.svs.GeoPoint
import com.benomad.msdk.core.svs.StringAttribute

const val POI_POINT_ID = 12001L //ID for the POIs: a custom class ID, which has the POI style created above

// In the Activity/Fragment that implements OnMapReadyCallback:
private lateinit var dynamicLayerGroup: DynamicLayersGroup //group of layers that will be attached to the MapView

private val geoPoint = GeoPoint(3.24, 43.6)
private val secondGeoPoint = GeoPoint(2.10, 42.5)

override fun onMapReady() {
    dynamicLayerGroup = DynamicLayersGroup() //the map is ready, so the Core is initialized

    dynamicLayerGroup.newPoint(POI_POINT_ID, geoPoint, emptyArray()) //add a point to the group of layers with no attributes (emptyArray)

    val atts = arrayOf<Attribute>(StringAttribute(CartoConst.KB_ATT_NAME, "Second POI"))
    dynamicLayerGroup.newPoint(POI_POINT_ID, secondGeoPoint, atts) //add a second point with the same classID (same style and same z-order) but with a label

    mapView.attachDynamicLayers(dynamicLayerGroup) //attach the group of layers to the MapView. The layers of the group will be rendered on the MapView
}
```

Later, you can detach the group, attach it again, and change its layers:

``` kotlin
mapView.detachDynamicLayers() //detach the group of layers from the MapView. Layers are not visible anymore on the MapView
mapView.attachDynamicLayers(dynamicLayerGroup) //reattach layers

dynamicLayerGroup.remove(POI_POINT_ID) //remove the two created points from the group of layers (as they have the same class ID). The points won't be visible on the MapView anymore (as the dynamicLayerGroup is attached to the MapView)

dynamicLayerGroup.newPoint(POI_POINT_ID, geoPoint, emptyArray()) //add a point to the group of layers that is already attached to the MapView. The point is now visible on the map 

dynamicLayerGroup.newPoint(POI_POINT_ID, secondGeoPoint, emptyArray()) //add a second point
```

### Types of layers

- Point
- Line
- Polyline
- Rectangle
- Ellipse
- Polygon
- Corridor

See the `DynamicLayersGroup` class of the Core module for the details. For a custom layer, provide your own SVS form, created with the `Form` abstract class of the Core module.

## Create a numbered POIs style

A `POIStyle` can draw a number at the center of the POI's icon. Create it with `textFromAttributeCode` set to `CartoConst.KB_ATT_FEATURE_CLASS_CODE`, and with an icon. The icon can be one of the map resources that the Core deploys from the assets to the app's external scoped storage (see the **Core initialization** section of the Core module).

```kotlin

import android.graphics.Color
import android.util.Log
import com.benomad.msdk.core.carto.CartoConst
import com.benomad.msdk.mapping.style.MapStyle
import com.benomad.msdk.mapping.style.POIStyle
import com.benomad.msdk.mapping.MapView

/**
* Creates a numbered POI style
* @param classID the classID for which the style is defined (same classID will be used when creating points)
* @param iconPath the absolute path to the icon (the number will be set at the center of that icon)
* @param style the [MapStyle] of the [MapView]
*/
fun createNumberedPOIStyle(classID: Long, iconPath: String, style: MapStyle): com.benomad.msdk.errormanager.Error? {
    val err = style.createPOIStyle(classID, POIStyle().apply {
        textFromAttributeCode = CartoConst.KB_ATT_FEATURE_CLASS_CODE
        fontColor = Color.WHITE //set color of the number
        icon = iconPath
    })
    if (err != null) {
        Log.e("NumberedPOIStyle", "Numbered POI style creation error : ${err.messageId} - ${err.detailedMessage}")
    }
    return err
}
```

Then create a POI with the same class ID:

``` kotlin
import com.benomad.msdk.core.carto.CartoConst
import com.benomad.msdk.core.svs.UnSignedAttribute

val number = 3L // the number drawn on the icon: an UnSignedAttribute holds a Long
dynamicLayerGroup.newPoint(NUMBERED_POI_CLASS_ID, point, arrayOf(UnSignedAttribute(CartoConst.KB_ATT_FEATURE_CLASS_CODE, number))) // NUMBERED_POI_CLASS_ID: the classID given to createNumberedPOIStyle; point: the GeoPoint of the POI
```

The point is drawn with the icon and the number at its center. The `POIStyle` class in the API reference lists all the POI style options.

## Layers clustering

Clustering is enabled per class ID. For example, with clustering enabled for `POI_POINT_ID` (from the example above), all the layers of the `MapView` with this class ID are grouped into clusters, depending on their position on the map and on the zoom level. A cluster groups at least 3 layers, and by default its icon shows how many.

To enable clustering for points of the same class ID (continuing the example above):

``` kotlin
val ids = listOf(POI_POINT_ID.toInt()) //the cluster methods take the class IDs as Int values

mapView?.createPOICluster("cluster_name_identifier",
                          ids, //the list of class IDs that defines which layers will be clustered
                          null, //an optional Bitmap image to change the cluster appearance
                          0xFFA500FF.toInt(), //RGBA color (0xRRGGBBAA, here orange) for the text, and for the icon if no custom icon is provided
                          1.2) //the scale of the icon shown for the cluster

mapView?.removePOICluster("cluster_name_identifier") //disable the clustering
```

With several class IDs, the clusters mix the layers of all these class IDs.

## Map interactions and events

To react to taps and long presses on the map, listen to click events: each one tells you what was clicked (POIs, routes, clusters or dynamic layer objects).

### Setting up a map click listener

Implement `OnMapClickedListener` and register it with the `MapView`:

``` kotlin
val mapClickedListener = object : OnMapClickedListener {
    override fun onMapTap(results: MapClickedResults) {
        // User tapped on the map
        handleMapClick(results)
    }

    override fun onMapLongPress(results: MapClickedResults) {
        // User long pressed on the map
        handleMapLongPress(results)
    }
}

// Register the listener for both tap and long press events
mapView.setMapClickedListener(mapClickedListener, tap = true, longPress = true)

// You can also register only for tap events
mapView.setMapClickedListener(mapClickedListener, tap = true, longPress = false)

// Or only for long press events
mapView.setMapClickedListener(mapClickedListener, tap = false, longPress = true)

// To unregister the listener
mapView.setMapClickedListener(null, tap = false, longPress = false)
```

### MapClickedResults

Each click event comes with a `MapClickedResults`:

``` kotlin
data class MapClickedResults(
    val addresses: List<Address>?,        // POIs found near the clicked point, or the address of the road there
    val clusters: List<ClusterResult>?,   // POI clusters that were clicked
    val objects: List<ClickedObject>?     // Map objects within 10 m of the clicked point (dynamic layer forms, a displayed route)
)
```

- When the search at the clicked location could run, `addresses` is never null: it can be empty, and holds the address of the road at the clicked location when no POI and no cluster is found.
- `clusters` and `objects` are null when nothing of their kind was found.
- All three fields are null only when the search couldn't run, for example because a previous search was still running: it doesn't mean that nothing is there.

### Clicked addresses

`addresses` holds the POIs found near the clicked point, the nearest first, 10 at most. When there is neither a POI nor a cluster there, it holds the address of the road at that point. A route shown on the map is reported in `objects`.

``` kotlin
override fun onMapTap(results: MapClickedResults) {
    results.addresses?.forEach { address ->
        // An Address object contains information about the clicked POI or road
        val name = address.name
        val road = address.road
        val city = address.city
        // See the Address class in the Geocoder module for all available fields
    }
}
```

### Clicked clusters

`clusters` describes the POI clusters that were clicked:

``` kotlin
data class ClusterResult(
    val id: List<Int>,                    // Class IDs of the POIs grouped in the cluster
    val bbox: GeoRect,                    // Bounding box of the cluster
    val pos: GeoPoint,                    // Geographic position of the cluster
    val addresses: List<Address>          // Addresses contained in the cluster
)
```

For example:

``` kotlin
override fun onMapTap(results: MapClickedResults) {
    results.clusters?.forEach { cluster ->
        val clusterPosition = cluster.pos
        val clusterSize = cluster.addresses.size
        val boundingBox = cluster.bbox

        // You can zoom on the cluster or show a list of addresses
        cluster.addresses.forEach { address ->
            // Handle each address in the cluster
        }
    }
}
```

### Clicked objects

`objects` describes the map objects that were clicked: dynamic layer objects (your POIs, polylines, polygons, etc.) or a route shown on the map. An object is reported only if its class is visible at the current scale, and if its class ID is between 1500 and 3999, above 9990, or one of the route and traffic-flow classes (6900, 6903, 6904, 6905, 6907 and 6910). The `CartoConst` class of the Core module lists most of the class IDs of the maps.

``` kotlin
data class ClickedObject(
    val objectID: ObjectId,               // Unique identifier of the clicked object
    val attributes: List<Attribute>       // Attributes associated with the object
)
```

For example:

``` kotlin
override fun onMapTap(results: MapClickedResults) {
    results.objects?.forEach { clickedObject ->
        val objectId = clickedObject.objectID

        // Access attributes of the clicked object
        clickedObject.attributes.forEach { attribute ->
            when (attribute) {
                is StringAttribute -> {
                    val value = attribute.value
                    // Handle string attribute
                }
                is UnSignedAttribute -> {
                    val value = attribute.value
                    // Handle unsigned attribute
                }
                // Handle other attribute types
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Complete example

Handling every kind of click result:

``` kotlin
import android.os.Bundle
import android.view.LayoutInflater
import android.view.View
import android.view.ViewGroup
import androidx.fragment.app.Fragment
import com.benomad.msdk.errormanager.Error // the Error class of the MSDK, not kotlin.Error
import com.benomad.msdk.mapping.MapView
import com.benomad.msdk.mapping.callbacks.OnMapClickedListener
import com.benomad.msdk.mapping.callbacks.OnMapReadyCallback
import com.benomad.msdk.mapping.results.MapClickedResults

class MapFragment : Fragment(), OnMapReadyCallback {
    private lateinit var mapView: MapView

    override fun onCreateView(inflater: LayoutInflater, container: ViewGroup?, savedInstanceState: Bundle?): View? {
        mapView = MapView(requireContext(), callback = this)
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycle.addObserver(mapView)
        return mapView // the MapView is the view of this fragment: its map is created once it is attached, visible and laid out
    }

    override fun onMapReady() {
        // Map is ready, setup the clicked listener
        val mapClickedListener = object : OnMapClickedListener {
            override fun onMapTap(results: MapClickedResults) {
                handleClickResults(results, isLongPress = false)
            }

            override fun onMapLongPress(results: MapClickedResults) {
                handleClickResults(results, isLongPress = true)
            }
        }

        mapView.setMapClickedListener(mapClickedListener, tap = true, longPress = true)
    }

    private fun handleClickResults(results: MapClickedResults, isLongPress: Boolean) {
        val clickType = if (isLongPress) "Long press" else "Tap"

        // Handle clicked addresses (POIs or road)
        results.addresses?.let { addresses ->
            println("$clickType: ${addresses.size} address(es) clicked")
            addresses.forEach { address ->
                println("  - ${address.name} at ${address.city}")
            }
        }

        // Handle clicked clusters
        results.clusters?.let { clusters ->
            println("$clickType: ${clusters.size} cluster(s) clicked")
            clusters.forEach { cluster ->
                println("  - Cluster with ${cluster.addresses.size} addresses")
                println("    Position: ${cluster.pos}")
            }
        }

        // Handle clicked dynamic layer objects
        results.objects?.let { objects ->
            println("$clickType: ${objects.size} object(s) clicked")
            objects.forEach { clickedObject ->
                println("  - Object ID: ${clickedObject.objectID}")
                clickedObject.attributes.forEach { attribute ->
                    println("    Attribute ${attribute.code}: $attribute")
                }
            }
        }

        // If the search could not run (for example because a previous search was still running), the three lists are null
        if (results.addresses == null) {
            println("$clickType: the search could not run at this location")
        }
    }

    override fun onMapError(error: Error) {
        // Handle error
    }
}
```
